Childs.Title: "EXTRA" CLASS
Childs.Definition: Products in this class must be of superior quality. They must be characteristic of the variety and/or commercial type specified. Depending on the nature of the produce specific provisions can apply as specified in the UNECE Standards for Fresh Fruit and vegetables. They must be free from defects, with the exception of very slight superficial defects, provided these do not affect the general appearance of the produce, the quality, the keeping quality and presentation in the package.

Childs.Title: CLASS I
Childs.Definition: Products in this class must be of good quality. They must be characteristic of the variety and/or commercial type. There can be specific provisions, depending on the nature of the produce as specified in the UNECE Standards for Fresh Fruit and vegetables. Slight defects, however, may be allowed, provided these do not affect the general appearance of the produce, the quality, the keeping quality and presentation in the package:- a slight defect in shape- slight defects in colouring- slight skin defects.

Childs.Title: CLASS II
Childs.Definition: This class includes products that do not qualify for inclusion in a higher classes but satisfy the minimum requirements for this product as specified in the UNECE Standards for Fresh Fruit and vegetables. The following defects may be allowed, provided the produce retain their essential characteristics as regards the quality, the keeping quality and presentation:- defects in shape- defects in colouring- skin defects.

Childs.Title: Quality (UNECE Standard)
Childs.Definition: Indicates, with reference to the product branding, labelling or packaging, the descriptive term that is used by the product manufacturer to identify the quality classification or category according to Codex Alimentarius or UNECE standards. UNCLASSIFIED applies to fruits that are not yet packed (e.g. delivery of a grower to a pack house) or not qualified to be sold as fresh fruits in the target market since they do not meet the specifications required by legislation.

Childs.Title: "EXTRA" CLASS
Childs.Definition: Products in this class must be of superior quality. They must be characteristic of the variety and/or commercial type specified. Depending on the nature of the produce specific provisions can apply as specified in the UNECE Standards for Fresh Fruit and vegetables. They must be free from defects, with the exception of very slight superficial defects, provided these do not affect the general appearance of the produce, the quality, the keeping quality and presentation in the package.

Childs.Title: CLASS I
Childs.Definition: Products in this class must be of good quality. They must be characteristic of the variety and/or commercial type. There can be specific provisions, depending on the nature of the produce as specified in the UNECE Standards for Fresh Fruit and vegetables. Slight defects, however, may be allowed, provided these do not affect the general appearance of the produce, the quality, the keeping quality and presentation in the package:- a slight defect in shape- slight defects in colouring- slight skin defects.

Childs.Title: CLASS II
Childs.Definition: This class includes products that do not qualify for inclusion in a higher classes but satisfy the minimum requirements for this product as specified in the UNECE Standards for Fresh Fruit and vegetables. The following defects may be allowed, provided the produce retain their essential characteristics as regards the quality, the keeping quality and presentation:- defects in shape- defects in colouring- skin defects.

Childs.Definition: Products in this class must be of superior quality. They must be characteristic of the variety and/or commercial type specified. They must be free from defects, with the exception of very slight superficial defects, provided these do not affect the general appearance of the produce, the quality, the keeping quality and presentation in the package.

Childs.Title: CLASS I

Childs.Title: CLASS II
Childs.Definition: This class includes products that do not qualify for inclusion in a higher classes but satisfy the minimum requirements for this product as specified in the UNECE Standards for Fresh Fruit and vegetables. Childs.Title: ORGANIC

Childs.Title: TRANSITIONAL

Childs.Title: UNIDENTIFIED

Childs.Title: Quality (UNECE Standard)
Childs.Definition: Indicates, with reference to the product branding, labelling or packaging, the descriptive term that is used by the product manufacturer to identify the quality classification or category according to Codex Alimentarius or UNECE standards. UNCLASSIFIED applies to fruits that are not yet packed (e.g. delivery of a grower to a pack house) or not qualified to be sold as fresh fruits in the target market since they do not meet the specifications required by legislation.

Childs.Title: "EXTRA" CLASS
Childs.Definition: Products in this class must be of superior quality. They must be characteristic of the variety and/or commercial type specified. Depending on the nature of the produce specific provisions can apply as specified in the UNECE Standards for Fresh Fruit and vegetables. They must be free from defects, with the exception of very slight superficial defects, provided these do not affect the general appearance of the produce, the quality, the keeping quality and presentation in the package.

Childs.Title: CLASS I
Childs.Definition: Products in this class must be of good quality. They must be characteristic of the variety and/or commercial type. There can be specific provisions, depending on the nature of the produce as specified in the UNECE Standards for Fresh Fruit and vegetables. Slight defects, however, may be allowed, provided these do not affect the general appearance of the produce, the quality, the keeping quality and presentation in the package:- a slight defect in shape- slight defects in colouring- slight skin defects.

Childs.Title: CLASS II
Childs.Definition: This class includes products that do not qualify for inclusion in a higher classes but satisfy the minimum requirements for this product as specified in the UNECE Standards for Fresh Fruit and vegetables. The following defects may be allowed, provided the produce retain their essential characteristics as regards the quality, the keeping quality and presentation:- defects in shape- defects in colouring- skin defects.

Childs.Title: Cooking Type Of Potatoes
Childs.Definition: Indicates, with reference to the product branding, labelling or packaging, the descriptive term that is used by the manufacturer that specifies the cooking characteristics of potatoes . For culinary purposes, varieties are often described in terms of their waxiness.

Childs.Title: FLOURY
Childs.Definition: High starch/low moisture potatoes are also described as having high solids. Also referred to as Creamy. They have a dry matter (starch content) of 22% or greater. In some varieties based on climate this amount starts at 26% dry matter. Ideal for jacket and boiled potatoes, mashed potatoes, dumplings, stews and soups.

Childs.Title: PREDOMINANTLY WAXY
Childs.Definition: Lower starch potatoes than waxy and absorb less water when cooked. These are usually new or young potatoes. They can have a dry matter of 14% or less but that is subjective. The supplier of the potatoes ultimately determines the cooking type. Ideal for boiled and jacket potatoes, as well as fried and grilled potatoes, stews, casseroles, soups, and fritters.

Childs.Title: Quality (UNECE Standard)
Childs.Definition: Indicates, with reference to the product branding, labelling or packaging, the descriptive term that is used by the product manufacturer to identify the quality classification or category according to Codex Alimentarius or UNECE standards. UNCLASSIFIED applies to fruits that are not yet packed (e.g. delivery of a grower to a pack house) or not qualified to be sold as fresh fruits in the target market since they do not meet the specifications required by legislation.

Childs.Title: "EXTRA" CLASS
Childs.Definition: Products in this class must be of superior quality. They must be characteristic of the variety and/or commercial type specified. Depending on the nature of the produce specific provisions can apply as specified in the UNECE Standards for Fresh Fruit and vegetables. They must be free from defects, with the exception of very slight superficial defects, provided these do not affect the general appearance of the produce, the quality, the keeping quality and presentation in the package.

Childs.Title: CLASS I
Childs.Definition: Products in this class must be of good quality. They must be characteristic of the variety and/or commercial type. There can be specific provisions, depending on the nature of the produce as specified in the UNECE Standards for Fresh Fruit and vegetables. Slight defects, however, may be allowed, provided these do not affect the general appearance of the produce, the quality, the keeping quality and presentation in the package:- a slight defect in shape- slight defects in colouring- slight skin defects.

Childs.Title: CLASS II
Childs.Definition: This class includes products that do not qualify for inclusion in a higher classes but satisfy the minimum requirements for this product as specified in the UNECE Standards for Fresh Fruit and vegetables. The following defects may be allowed, provided the produce retain their essential characteristics as regards the quality, the keeping quality and presentation:- defects in shape- defects in colouring- skin defects.

Childs.Title: Quality (UNECE Standard)
Childs.Definition: Indicates, with reference to the product branding, labelling or packaging, the descriptive term that is used by the product manufacturer to identify the quality classification or category according to Codex Alimentarius or UNECE standards. UNCLASSIFIED applies to fruits that are not yet packed (e.g. delivery of a grower to a pack house) or not qualified to be sold as fresh fruits in the target market since they do not meet the specifications required by legislation.

Childs.Title: "EXTRA" CLASS
Childs.Definition: Products in this class must be of superior quality. They must be characteristic of the variety and/or commercial type specified. Depending on the nature of the produce specific provisions can apply as specified in the UNECE Standards for Fresh Fruit and vegetables. They must be free from defects, with the exception of very slight superficial defects, provided these do not affect the general appearance of the produce, the quality, the keeping quality and presentation in the package.

Childs.Title: CLASS I
Childs.Definition: Products in this class must be of good quality. They must be characteristic of the variety and/or commercial type. There can be specific provisions, depending on the nature of the produce as specified in the UNECE Standards for Fresh Fruit and vegetables. Slight defects, however, may be allowed, provided these do not affect the general appearance of the produce, the quality, the keeping quality and presentation in the package:- a slight defect in shape- slight defects in colouring- slight skin defects.

Childs.Title: CLASS II
Childs.Definition: This class includes products that do not qualify for inclusion in a higher classes but satisfy the minimum requirements for this product as specified in the UNECE Standards for Fresh Fruit and vegetables. The following defects may be allowed, provided the produce retain their essential characteristics as regards the quality, the keeping quality and presentation:- defects in shape- defects in colouring- skin defects.

Childs.Title: Quality (UNECE Standard)
Childs.Definition: Indicates, with reference to the product branding, labelling or packaging, the descriptive term that is used by the product manufacturer to identify the quality classification or category according to Codex Alimentarius or UNECE standards. UNCLASSIFIED applies to fruits that are not yet packed (e.g. delivery of a grower to a pack house) or not qualified to be sold as fresh fruits in the target market since they do not meet the specifications required by legislation.

Childs.Title: "EXTRA" CLASS
Childs.Definition: Products in this class must be of superior quality. They must be characteristic of the variety and/or commercial type specified. Depending on the nature of the produce specific provisions can apply as specified in the UNECE Standards for Fresh Fruit and vegetables. They must be free from defects, with the exception of very slight superficial defects, provided these do not affect the general appearance of the produce, the quality, the keeping quality and presentation in the package.

Childs.Title: CLASS I
Childs.Definition: Products in this class must be of good quality. They must be characteristic of the variety and/or commercial type. There can be specific provisions, depending on the nature of the produce as specified in the UNECE Standards for Fresh Fruit and vegetables. Slight defects, however, may be allowed, provided these do not affect the general appearance of the produce, the quality, the keeping quality and presentation in the package:- a slight defect in shape- slight defects in colouring- slight skin defects.

Childs.Title: CLASS II
Childs.Definition: This class includes products that do not qualify for inclusion in a higher classes but satisfy the minimum requirements for this product as specified in the UNECE Standards for Fresh Fruit and vegetables. The following defects may be allowed, provided the produce retain their essential characteristics as regards the quality, the keeping quality and presentation:- defects in shape- defects in colouring- skin defects.

Childs.Title: "EXTRA" CLASS
Childs.Definition: Products in this class must be of superior quality. They must be characteristic of the variety and/or commercial type specified. They must be free from defects, with the exception of very slight superficial defects, provided these do not affect the general appearance of the produce, the quality, the keeping quality and presentation in the package.

Childs.Title: CLASS II

Childs.Title: Quality (UNECE Standard)

UNCLASSIFIED applies to fruits that are not yet packed (e.g. delivery of a grower to a pack house) or not qualified to be sold as fresh fruits in the target market since they do not meet the specifications required by legislation.

Childs.Title: "EXTRA" CLASS
Childs.Definition: Products in this class must be of superior quality. They must be characteristic of the variety and/or commercial type specified. Depending on the nature of the produce specific provisions can apply as specified in the UNECE Standards for Fresh Fruit and vegetables. They must be free from defects, with the exception of very slight superficial defects, provided these do not affect the general appearance of the produce, the quality, the keeping quality and presentation in the package.

Childs.Title: CLASS I
Childs.Definition: Products in this class must be of good quality. They must be characteristic of the variety and/or commercial type. There can be specific provisions, depending on the nature of the produce as specified in the UNECE Standards for Fresh Fruit and vegetables. Slight defects, however, may be allowed, provided these do not affect the general appearance of the produce, the quality, the keeping quality and presentation in the package:- a slight defect in shape- slight defects in colouring- slight skin defects.

Childs.Title: CLASS II
Childs.Definition: This class includes products that do not qualify for inclusion in a higher classes but satisfy the minimum requirements for this product as specified in the UNECE Standards for Fresh Fruit and vegetables. The following defects may be allowed, provided the produce retain their essential characteristics as regards the quality, the keeping quality and presentation:- defects in shape- defects in colouring- skin defects.

Childs.Title: CLASS I

Childs.Title: PLASTIC
Childs.Definition: Plastic is a material consisting of any of a wide range of synthetic or semi-synthetic organics that are malleable and can be molded into solid objects of diverse shapes. Plastics are typically organic polymers of high molecular mass, but they often contain other substances. They are usually synthetic, most commonly derived from petrochemicals, but many are partially natural. Plasticity is the general property of all materials that are able to irreversibly deform without breaking, but this occurs to such a degree with this class of moldable polymers that their name is an emphasis on this ability.

Childs.Title: SILICONE/GEL
Childs.Definition: Silicones are polymers that include any inert, synthetic compound made up of repeating units of siloxane, which is a chain of alternating silicon atoms and oxygen atoms, frequently combined with carbon and/or hydrogen. They are typically heat-resistant and rubber-like, and are used in sealants, adhesives, lubricants, medicine, cooking utensils, and thermal and electrical insulation. Some common forms include silicone oil, silicone grease, silicone rubber, silicone resin, and silicone caulk.

Childs.Title: PLASTIC
Childs.Definition: Plastic is a material consisting of any of a wide range of synthetic or semi-synthetic organics that are malleable and can be molded into solid objects of diverse shapes. Plastics are typically organic polymers of high molecular mass, but they often contain other substances. They are usually synthetic, most commonly derived from petrochemicals, but many are partially natural. Plasticity is the general property of all materials that are able to irreversibly deform without breaking, but this occurs to such a degree with this class of moldable polymers that their name is an emphasis on this ability.

Childs.Title: SILICONE/GEL
Childs.Definition: Silicones are polymers that include any inert, synthetic compound made up of repeating units of siloxane, which is a chain of alternating silicon atoms and oxygen atoms, frequently combined with carbon and/or hydrogen. They are typically heat-resistant and rubber-like, and are used in sealants, adhesives, lubricants, medicine, cooking utensils, and thermal and electrical insulation. Some common forms include silicone oil, silicone grease, silicone rubber, silicone resin, and silicone caulk.

They are usually synthetic, most commonly derived from petrochemicals, but many are partially natural. They are usually synthetic, most commonly derived from petrochemicals, but many are partially natural. Childs.Title: PLASTIC
Childs.Definition: Plastic is a material consisting of any of a wide range of synthetic or semi-synthetic organics that are malleable and can be molded into solid objects of diverse shapes. Plastics are typically organic polymers of high molecular mass, but they often contain other substances. They are usually synthetic, most commonly derived from petrochemicals, but many are partially natural. Plasticity is the general property of all materials that are able to irreversibly deform without breaking, but this occurs to such a degree with this class of moldable polymers that their name is an emphasis on this ability.

Childs.Title: Type of Finish
Childs.Definition: Indicate, with reference to the product branding, labelling or packaging, the descriptive term that is used by the product manufacturer to identify whether the product is designed with matt or gloss finish.

Childs.Title: ANTIQUE
Childs.Definition: The item has been finished with a process whereby the item has been painted, glazed, dinged, pitted, rubbed, or otherwise made to show wear and use patterns. These patterns provide the impression that the item is older than it is.

Childs.Title: BRUSHED
Childs.Definition: The item has been finished with a process whereby marks on the surface either from sanding, as in metal surfaces, or by bristle marks, as in painted or finished surfaces.

Childs.Title: COMBINATION FINISH
Childs.Definition: The item has been finished using a combination of several different finishing methods such as, but not limited to Polishing, Flaming, Glazing, or Oil Rubbing.

Childs.Title: DRYING OILS
Childs.Definition: The item has been finished with a process whereby the item was rubbed with oils such linseed or tugsten oil, parafin or beeswax.

Childs.Title: FLAMED
Childs.Definition: The item has been finished with a process whereby the item was subjected to flames or fire to provide a scorched or burned look.

Childs.Title: GLAZED
Childs.Definition: The item has been finished with a glaze to provide a lustrous or glassy appearance. This finish may or may not be fired in a kiln, depending on the material to which it is applied.

Childs.Title: GLOSS
Childs.Definition: The finish of the item has an optical property on the surface to reflect light in a specular or mirror-like direction. (Greater than a 70% gloss)

Childs.Title: MATT
Childs.Definition: The finish of the item has an optical property on the surface of a dull or no-luster sheen. (0 to 10% gloss)

Childs.Title: POLISHED
Childs.Definition: The item has been finished with a process whereby the item was ground and buffed typically with machines and polishing compounds.

Childs.Title: PREFINISHED
Childs.Definition: The item is already finished by the manufacturer and requires no other finishing by the end user.

Childs.Title: PRIMED
Childs.Definition: The item has been painted with a primer paint by the manufacturer and is ready to be painted with the finish colour by the end user.

Childs.Title: RAW/NO FINISH
Childs.Definition: The item has not been painted or finished by the manufacturer and is ready to be painted finished by the end user.

Childs.Title: SATIN
Childs.Definition: The finish of the item has an optical property on the surface of a extremely low to no-luster sheen, although it is not as dull as a Matte finish. (25-35% gloss)

Childs.Title: SILK/SEMI-GLOSS/SATINWOOD
Childs.Definition: The finish of the item has an optical property on the surface of a low-luster sheen. (35 to 70% gloss)

Childs.Title: UNCLASSIFIED
Childs.Definition: This term is used to describe those product attributes that are unable to be classified within their specific market; e.g. goat's cheese - goat's cheeses is often generically labelled and cannot be further classified.

Childs.Title: UNGLAZED
Childs.Definition: The item has not been finished with a glaze to provide a lustrous or glassy appearance.

Childs.Title: BAMBOO
Childs.Definition: A flowering perennial evergreen plant in the grass family Poaceae, subfamily Bambusoideae, tribe Bambuseae.

Childs.Title: BUTCHER BLOCK
Childs.Definition: Edge grain butcher block tops have parallel wood rails that run the length of the piece. End grain butcher block tops are created by fusing together the end pieces of wood rails into a checkerboard pattern.

Childs.Title: COMPRESSED PAPER OR FIBRE
Childs.Definition: Paper composite countertops are made of post-consumer recycled paper and other fibers held together by a formaldehyde-free thermoset plastic resin. Available in thicknesses ranging from 1 inch to 2 inches.

Childs.Title: CONCRETE- CAST IN PLACE
Childs.Definition: A composite material composed of coarse granular material (the aggregate or filler) embedded in a hard matrix of material (the cement or binder) that fills the space among the aggregate particles and glues them together. This product is cast at the installation site.

Childs.Title: CONCRETE- PRECAST
Childs.Definition: A construction product produced by casting concrete in a reusable mold or "form" which is then cured in a controlled environment, transported to the construction site and put into place.

Childs.Title: CONCRETE- PROCESSED SLABS
Childs.Definition: A common structural element of slabs of steel reinforced concrete.

Childs.Title: CORK
Childs.Definition: Cork is a material that is harvested for commercial use primarily from the bark of the Cork Oak tree.

Childs.Title: GABBRO
Childs.Definition: A large group of dark, coarse-grained, intrusive mafic igneous rocks chemically equivalent to basalt.

Childs.Title: GLASS - RECYCLED
Childs.Definition: Glass which as been recylced from other uses and crushed or refired for purposes of subsequent use.

Childs.Title: GLASS- CRAFTED
Childs.Definition: Glass of various colours, hues and shapes which have been moulded together for use.

Childs.Title: GRANITE
Childs.Definition: Granite is a igneous rock that contains at least 20% quartz by volume, but also some mica and feldspar.

Childs.Title: HIGH-DENSITY POLYETHYLENE (HDPE)
Childs.Definition: High-Density Polyethylene (HDPE) is a polyethylene thermoplastic made from petroleum. A strong, relatively opaque form of polyethylene having a dense structure with few side branches off the main carbon backbone. Can be applied to bottles, flasks and caps.

Childs.Title: LAVA
Childs.Definition: Volcanic lava stone is extracted by hand from open-air quarries, then cut into slabs, glazed with enamel, and fired in a kiln at 1300 degrees. During cooling a smooth crackled finish develops.

Childs.Title: LEATHER
Childs.Definition: Leather is a durable and flexible material created by tanning animal rawhide and skin, often cattle hide.

Childs.Title: LIMESTONE
Childs.Definition: A sedimentary rock composed largely of the minerals calcite and aragonite, which are different crystal forms of calcium carbonate(CaCO3).

Childs.Title: MELAMINE
Childs.Definition: An organic base and a trimer of cyanamide, with a 1,3,5-triazine skeleton.

Childs.Title: PALM WOOD
Childs.Definition: Arecaceae or are a botanical family of perennial lianas, shrubs, and trees commonly known as palm trees.

Childs.Title: QUARTZ- ENGINEERED
Childs.Definition: Quartz countertops are man-made engineered stone countertops formed by combining 90% ground quartz (a natural hard mineral) with 8-10% resins, polymers, and pigments. This forms a very hard granite-like surface. The appearance depends on how the quartz is ground: coarsely ground quartz produces a flecked appearance, while finely ground quartz produces a smooth look.

Childs.Title: SOAPSTONE
Childs.Definition: Soapstone is a natural stone, like granite, that is quarried. It's composed mostly of mineral talc, which makes it quite soft, but soapstone used for countertops typically has higher percentages of quartz in it, which makes it harder and more suitable as a kitchen surface.

Childs.Title: SOLID SURFACES MATERIALS
Childs.Definition: Synthetic or manufactured solid surface countertops are made of man-made materials, most often acrylic, but also polyester resins, marble dust, and other pigments.

Childs.Title: STAINLESS STEEL
Childs.Definition: Stainless steel is made of a metal alloy with a chromium content around 10 percent.

Childs.Title: TERRAZZO
Childs.Definition: A composite material, poured in place or precast, consisting of marble, quartz, granite, glass, or other suitable chips, sprinkled or unsprinkled, and poured with a binder that is cementitious, chemical, or a combination of both. Terrazzo is cured and then ground and polished to a smooth surface or otherwise finished to produce a uniformly textured surface.

Childs.Title: TILE- CERAMIC
Childs.Definition: Ceramic tile is made from clay, which is fired at a high temperature.

Childs.Title: TILE- GLASS
Childs.Definition: Pieces of glass formed into consistent shapes.

Childs.Title: TILE- NATURAL STONE
Childs.Definition: Pieces of stone formed into consistent shapes as opposed to cut from large slabs.

Childs.Title: TRAVERTINE
Childs.Definition: A form of limestone deposited by mineral springs, especially hot springs. Travertine often has a fibrous or concentric appearance and exists in white, tan, and cream-colored varieties.

Childs.Definition: Processed wood retrieved from its original application for purposes of subsequent use.

Childs.Title: ZINC
Childs.Definition: Zinc bears a dull, slightly mottled surface that has more in common with pewter than with chrome or stainless steel. It looks seasoned even when it's new, and it has an inherent warmth that many metals lack.

Childs.Title: PLASTIC
Childs.Definition: Plastic is a material consisting of any of a wide range of synthetic or semi-synthetic organics that are malleable and can be molded into solid objects of diverse shapes. Plastics are typically organic polymers of high molecular mass, but they often contain other substances. They are usually synthetic, most commonly derived from petrochemicals, but many are partially natural. Plasticity is the general property of all materials that are able to irreversibly deform without breaking, but this occurs to such a degree with this class of moldable polymers that their name is an emphasis on this ability.

Childs.Title: Fire Fighting Equipment
Childs.Definition: Includes any products that can be described/observed as components and technical devices used in the service of firefighters during firefighting and whose main purpose is to create protection against and in connection with fire. Includes products such as manifolds, hydrant valves, coupling parts.
Childs.DefinitionExcludes: Excludes products such as Fire Hydrant Systems.

Childs.Title: Fire Hydrant Systems
Childs.Definition: Includes any products that can be described/observed as a hydrant system which is a firefighting water supply that provides appropriate pressure and flows through a network of nozzles, pipelines, and hydrants throughout a structure. Hydrant boosters, fire pumps, and fire water pumps are all terms used to describe fire hydrant pump systems. These are high-pressure water pumps designed to increase the capability of construction firefighting by raising the force inside the hydrant service when the mains are insufficient. Irrigation and water transport are two of the most common uses for this system.
Childs.DefinitionExcludes: Excludes products such as Positive Displacement pumps, Centrifugal Pumps, Submersible Pumps and Pumps not specifically designed for use with Fluids.

Childs.Title: Submersible Pumps
Childs.Definition: Includes any products that can be described/observed as a mechanical device that pushes water toward the surface rather than drawing it away. It contains a hermetically sealed engine that helps to push the fluid toward the surface.
Childs.DefinitionExcludes: Excludes products such as Positive Displacement pumps, Centrifugal Pumps, Fire Hydrant Systems and Pumps not specifically designed for use with Fluids.

Childs.Title: Industrial Floating Footbridges
Childs.Definition: Includes any products that can be described/observed as a pedestrian bridge designed to connect two points. The device allow users to follow a certain path. It may be a movable or mounted device.
Childs.DefinitionExcludes: Excludes products such as stanchions.

Childs.Title: Industrial Floating Rafts
Childs.Definition: Includes any products that can be described/observed as a floating device. These floating devices are designed to accommodate a pump or an engine.
Childs.DefinitionExcludes: Excludes floating devices that are not specifically designed to support industrial pumps or engines.

Childs.Title: Industrial Floats
Childs.Definition: Includes any products that can be described/observed as plastic elements located between the raft and the dock or beach to support cables and pipes.
Childs.DefinitionExcludes: Excludes floats that are not specifically designed for industrial structures.

Childs.Title: Industrial Guardrails
Childs.Definition: Includes any products that can be described/observed as a guardrail or protective guarding designed to prevent or deter access to dangerous or off-limits areas. These safety element can be added to rafts, platforms, roads or ramps.
Childs.DefinitionExcludes: Excludes products such as footbridges.

Childs.Title: Industrial Raft Lids/Covers
Childs.Definition: Includes any products that can be described/observed as industrial raft cover or lid.
Childs.DefinitionExcludes: Excludes products such as complete Rafts.

Childs.Title: Industrial Structures

Childs.DefinitionExcludes: Excludes supporting structures that are not specifically designed to support industrial pumps and engines.

Childs.Definition: Includes any products that can be described/observed as an electric engine for industrial fluid pumps.
Childs.DefinitionExcludes: Excludes products such as combustion engines and any other engines not specifically designed for industrial fluid pumps.

Childs.Title: Industrial Pumps -Combustion Engines
Childs.Definition: Includes any products that can be described/observed as an combustion engine for industrial fluid pumps.
Childs.DefinitionExcludes: Excludes products such as electric engines and any other engines not specifically designed for industrial fluid pumps.

Childs.Title: Industrial Pumps - Replacement Parts/Accessories

Childs.DefinitionExcludes: Excludes any other replacement parts and accessories not specifically designed for industrial pumps.

Childs.Title: Type of Pump Replacement Part/Accessory
Childs.Definition: Indicates, with reference to the product branding, labelling or packaging, the descriptive term that is used by the product manufacturer to identify the type of pump replacement part or accessory.

Childs.Title: Pneumatics Pumps
Childs.Definition: Includes any products that can be described/observed as a pneumatic pump. Compressed air is used to move the liquid in pneumatic pumps. In pneumatic ejectors, compressed air displaces the liquid from a gravity-fed pressure vessel through a check valve into the discharge line in a series of surges spaced by the time required for the tank or receiver to fill again.
Childs.DefinitionExcludes: Excludes products such as Dynamic Pumps, Rotary Pumps, Reciprocating Pumps and Pumps not specifically designed for use with Fluids.

Childs.Title: Diaphragm Pumps
Childs.Definition: Includes any products that can be described/observed as a diaphragm pump. This pump uses two flexible diaphragms that move forward and backward to form a temporary vacuum through the pressure difference. This vacuum uses to introduce or discharge the liquid from the pump. The diaphragm acts as a partition wall between liquid and air.
Childs.DefinitionExcludes:
Excludes products such as Dynamic Pumps, Rotary Pumps, Pneumatic Pumps and Pumps not specifically designed for use with Fluids.
Specifically excludes other Reciprocating Pumps.

Childs.Title: Piston Pumps
Childs.Definition: Includes any products that can be described/observed as a piston pump. This pump mechanism consists of a reciprocating piston inside of a cylinder with check valves at both the intake and discharge. When the piston is on the suction stroke, the chamber inside of the cylinder expands, the pressure drops, the pressure valve on the suction side is opened, allowing fluid through the intake.
Childs.DefinitionExcludes:
Excludes products such as Dynamic Pumps, Rotary Pumps, Pneumatic Pumps and Pumps not specifically designed for use with Fluids.
Specifically excludes other Reciprocating Pumps.

Childs.Title: Plunger Pumps
Childs.Definition: Includes any products that can be described/observed as a plunger pump. A plunger pump works differently from a piston pump as the piston fits loosely in the cylinder, as opposed to a tight-fitting seal that a piston pump provides. The mass of the piston displaces the fluid in the cylinder as it is lowered, forcing it out the discharge side.
Childs.DefinitionExcludes:
Excludes products such as Dynamic Pumps, Rotary Pumps, Pneumatic Pumps and Pumps not specifically designed for use with Fluids.
Specifically excludes other Reciprocating Pumps.

Childs.Title: Gear Pumps
Childs.Definition: Includes any products that can be described/observed as a gear pump. A gear pump utilizes a pair of rotating gears inside a chamber (one gear driving the other) that moves and pushes the fluid out towards the other end of the pump. As the gears spin, it traps fluid between the gear teeth and the inside wall of the pump. The trapped fluid is then pushed in the direction the gear is spinning, eventually releasing out of the other side.
Childs.DefinitionExcludes:
Excludes products such as Dynamic Pumps, Reciprocating Pumps, Pneumatic Pumps and Pumps not specifically designed for use with Fluids.
Specifically excludes other Rotary Pumps.

Childs.Title: Lobe Pumps
Childs.Definition: Includes any products that can be described/observed as a lobe pump. The rotors in this pump are driven independently by external timing motors, instead of one rotor driving both of them as you’d find in gear pumps. The rotors have two or more lobes that rotate and trap fluid between the lobes, forcing fluid through the discharge outlet on each rotation.
Childs.DefinitionExcludes:
Excludes products such as Dynamic Pumps, Reciprocating Pumps, Pneumatic Pumps and Pumps not specifically designed for use with Fluids.
Specifically excludes other Rotary Pumps.

Childs.Title: Peristaltic/Roller Pumps
Childs.Definition: Includes any products that can be described/observed as a peristaltic pump. Peristaltic pumps contain fluid trapped in a flexible hose. The hose is pinched between the rollers and the inside wall of the housing. As the rollers revolve around a central axis, they squeeze the fluid through the tubes towards the discharge outlet, similar to what happens when you squeeze a tube of toothpaste at one end, and it squirts out the opening.
Childs.DefinitionExcludes:
Excludes products such as Dynamic Pumps, Reciprocating Pumps, Pneumatic Pumps and Pumps not specifically designed for use with Fluids.
Specifically excludes other Rotary Pumps.

Childs.Title: Progressive Cavity Pumps
Childs.Definition: Includes any products that can be described/observed as a progressive cavity pump. A progressive cavity pump contains a rotor rotating within a housing called a stator. The rotor is always metallic, and the stator is made up of a rubber type of material. The fluid is between the cavities and the rotary motion of the rotor forces the fluid through from one end to the other. It has a low to moderate capacity, low to high pressure, good solids handling capability, one seal, low shear, constant flow and a low pulsation.
Childs.DefinitionExcludes:
Excludes products such as Dynamic Pumps, Reciprocating Pumps, Pneumatic Pumps and Pumps not specifically designed for use with Fluids.
Specifically excludes other Rotary Pumps.

Childs.Title: Screw Pumps
Childs.Definition: Includes any products that can be described/observed as a screw pump. Screw pumps can have a single shaft with large threads on it, but it is more common to see two or three. The center shaft drives the other shafts like a screw gear. As the shaft rotates in the housing, fluid trapped in the gaps between the screw threads progresses along the length of the housing, then delivered to the discharge outlet.
Childs.DefinitionExcludes:
Excludes products such as Dynamic Pumps, Reciprocating Pumps, Pneumatic Pumps and Pumps not specifically designed for use with Fluids.
Specifically excludes other Rotary Pumps.

Childs.Title: Vane Pumps
Childs.Definition: Includes any products that can be described/observed as a vane pump. A vane pump rotor contains a series of slots for sliding vanes that press against the wall of the housing by centrifugal force when the rotor spins, forming a sealed chamber. Since the rotor is offset within the housing, the vanes extend and retract during rotation. When fluid is introduced, it is captured between the vanes as they are rotated, and directed to the discharge.
Childs.DefinitionExcludes:
Excludes products such as Dynamic Pumps, Reciprocating Pumps, Pneumatic Pumps and Pumps not specifically designed for use with Fluids.
Specifically excludes other Rotary Pumps.

Childs.Title: BAYONET CLOSURE
Childs.Definition: This term is used to describe a type of closure of pressure cooker. To close the lid, it is necessary to put the lid on the tank, then to turn the lid until the arrows drawn on the lid are aligned with arrows drawn on the tank.

Childs.Title: PUSH-BUTTON CLOSURE
Childs.Definition: This term is used to describe a type of closure of pressure cooker. To precede in the closure of the lid while assuring a perfect waterproofness of the device, it is just necessary to put the lid on the tank, and to press the big central button until this one jams.

Childs.Title: RE-ENTRANT LID CLOSURE
Childs.Definition: This term is used to describe a type of closure of pressure cooker. It is necessary to put the lid on the tank. Then, it is necessary to turn the lid until it jams. It looks like the system with bayonet, with the difference that the lid sits directly on the edges of the tank.

Childs.Title: STIRRUP CLOSURE
Childs.Definition: This term is used to describe a type of closure of pressure cooker consisting of a button of tightening and a stirrup fixed to the lid. The stirrup is a generally metallic part which crosses all the lid on its width. To close the lid, it is necessary to turn the button of tightening to lower the stirrup until it jams and until it closes the lid against the tank while assuring these two parts to stay stuck the one on the other one.

Childs.Definition: Earthenware is glazed or unglazed nonvitreous pottery which has normally been fired below 1200°C.

Childs.Title: PLASTIC
Childs.Definition: Plastic is a material consisting of any of a wide range of synthetic or semi-synthetic organics that are malleable and can be molded into solid objects of diverse shapes. Plastics are typically organic polymers of high molecular mass, but they often contain other substances. They are usually synthetic, most commonly derived from petrochemicals, but many are partially natural. Plasticity is the general property of all materials that are able to irreversibly deform without breaking, but this occurs to such a degree with this class of moldable polymers that their name is an emphasis on this ability.

Childs.Title: STONEWARE
Childs.Definition: Stoneware is a rather broad term for pottery or other ceramics fired at a relatively high temperature.

Childs.Title: Food Funnels

Childs.Title: KITCHEN FUNNEL

It is used to channel liquid or fine-grained substances into containers with a small opening, in order to avoid spillage. The material should be sturdy enough to withstand the weight of the substance being transferred.

Childs.Title: PISTON FUNNEL

They are made by a stiff enough material, not to crash under the weight of what we pour.

Childs.Title: PRESSURE SYRINGE

Childs.Title: PLASTIC
Childs.Definition: Plastic is a material consisting of any of a wide range of synthetic or semi-synthetic organics that are malleable and can be molded into solid objects of diverse shapes. Plastics are typically organic polymers of high molecular mass, but they often contain other substances. They are usually synthetic, most commonly derived from petrochemicals, but many are partially natural. Plasticity is the general property of all materials that are able to irreversibly deform without breaking, but this occurs to such a degree with this class of moldable polymers that their name is an emphasis on this ability.

Childs.Title: PLASTIC
Childs.Definition: Plastic is a material consisting of any of a wide range of synthetic or semi-synthetic organics that are malleable and can be molded into solid objects of diverse shapes. Plastics are typically organic polymers of high molecular mass, but they often contain other substances. They are usually synthetic, most commonly derived from petrochemicals, but many are partially natural. Childs.DefinitionExcludes: Excludes products such as Prams/Pushchairs that are used for transporting the baby and Highchairs that are used for feeding the babies. Specifically exclude products such as baby carriers, where the baby is transported by being strapped onto the front or the back of the carer.

Childs.Title: Baby Play Pens/Dens
Childs.Definition: Includes any products that can be described/observed as a safe structure in which a baby can play safely. Childs.DefinitionExcludes: Excludes products such as all Outdoor Play Structures such as Play Houses, Wendy Houses and Tree Houses, all Cots and Beds which may have similar safety features and all Carrying Cots, Cradles and Baskets.

A lifebuoy is usually ring-shaped or horseshoe-shaped and has a connecting line allowing the casualty to be pulled to the rescuer. A flotation cushion, upon which a body can float, is simply a cushion made of flotation foam covered in a waterproof material and has straps to enable rescue.

Childs.Title: Marine Electronic Chartplotters
Childs.Definition: Includes any products that can be described/observed as a device used in marine navigation that integrates GPS data with an electronic navigational chart to compute an accurate position of the vessel. These marine electronics devices are continuously evolving with larger screens, increased processing power, and multi-function capabilities that allow them to display data from a connected radar, fish finder, weather receiver, or be coupled to another marine chartplotter via a marine network.
Childs.DefinitionExcludes: Excludes products such as transponders, navigation radar equipment, navigation software and mobile GPS equipment used on land.

Childs.Title: Marine Navigation Radar Systems
Childs.Definition: Includes any products that can be described/observed as a system that provides navigation information when the vessel is within radar range of land or special radar aids. Distances and angular bearings are used to establish arcs of position and lines of position on a navigation chart.
Childs.DefinitionExcludes: Excludes products such as transponders, chartplotters, navigation software and mobile GPS equipment used on land.

Childs.Title: Marine Navigation Software
Childs.Definition: Includes any products that can be descrbed/observed as a computer-based navigation information system that complies with International Maritime Organization (IMO) regulations and can be used as an alternative to paper navigation charts. The system displays the information from electronic navigational charts and integrates position information from the Global Positioning System (GPS) and other navigational sensors, such as radar and automatic identification systems. It may also display additional navigation-related information, such as sailing directions and fathometer.
Childs.DefinitionExcludes: Excludes products such as transponders, chart plotters, radar systems and mobile GPS equipment used on land.

Childs.Title: PLASTIC
Childs.Definition: Plastic is a material consisting of any of a wide range of synthetic or semi-synthetic organics that are malleable and can be molded into solid objects of diverse shapes. Plastics are typically organic polymers of high molecular mass, but they often contain other substances. They are usually synthetic, most commonly derived from petrochemicals, but many are partially natural. Plasticity is the general property of all materials that are able to irreversibly deform without breaking, but this occurs to such a degree with this class of moldable polymers that their name is an emphasis on this ability.

Includes products such as corded and cordless sets as well as systems with automatic answering and door unlocking facilities.

Childs.Title: PLASTIC
Childs.Definition: Plastic is a material consisting of any of a wide range of synthetic or semi-synthetic organics that are malleable and can be molded into solid objects of diverse shapes. Plastics are typically organic polymers of high molecular mass, but they often contain other substances. They are usually synthetic, most commonly derived from petrochemicals, but many are partially natural. Plasticity is the general property of all materials that are able to irreversibly deform without breaking, but this occurs to such a degree with this class of moldable polymers that their name is an emphasis on this ability.

Childs.Title: PLASTIC
Childs.Definition: Plastic is a material consisting of any of a wide range of synthetic or semi-synthetic organics that are malleable and can be molded into solid objects of diverse shapes. Plastics are typically organic polymers of high molecular mass, but they often contain other substances. They are usually synthetic, most commonly derived from petrochemicals, but many are partially natural. Plasticity is the general property of all materials that are able to irreversibly deform without breaking, but this occurs to such a degree with this class of moldable polymers that their name is an emphasis on this ability.

Childs.Title: PLASTIC
Childs.Definition: Plastic is a material consisting of any of a wide range of synthetic or semi-synthetic organics that are malleable and can be molded into solid objects of diverse shapes. Plastics are typically organic polymers of high molecular mass, but they often contain other substances. They are usually synthetic, most commonly derived from petrochemicals, but many are partially natural. Plasticity is the general property of all materials that are able to irreversibly deform without breaking, but this occurs to such a degree with this class of moldable polymers that their name is an emphasis on this ability.

Childs.Title: BLACKBOARD
Childs.Definition: A blackboard (also known as a chalkboard) is a reusable writing surface on which text or drawings are made with sticks of calcium sulfate or calcium carbonate, known, when used for this purpose, as chalk. Blackboards were originally made of smooth, thin sheets of black or dark grey slate stone. Modern versions are often green because the colour is considered easier on the eyes.

Childs.Title: FRONT PROJECTION SCREEN
Childs.Definition: A front projection screen is an installation consisting of a surface and a support structure used for displaying a projected image from in front of the screen for the view of an audience. Projection screens may be permanently installed, as in a movie theater.

Childs.Title: PROJECTION SCREEN (FRONT AND REAR PROJECTION)
Childs.Definition: A projection screen (front and rear) is an installation consisting of a surface and a support structure used for displaying a projected image either from the front or rear of the screen for the view of an audience. Projection screens may be permanently installed, as in a movie theater.

Childs.Title: REAR PROJECTION SCREEN
Childs.Definition: A rear projection screen is an installation consisting of a surface and a support structure used for displaying a projected image from behind the screen for the view of an audience. Projection screens may be permanently installed, as in a movie theater.

Childs.Title: CORK
Childs.Definition: Cork is a material that is harvested for commercial use primarily from the bark of the Cork Oak tree.

Childs.Title: PLASTIC
Childs.Definition: Plastic is a material consisting of any of a wide range of synthetic or semi-synthetic organics that are malleable and can be molded into solid objects of diverse shapes. Plastics are typically organic polymers of high molecular mass, but they often contain other substances. They are usually synthetic, most commonly derived from petrochemicals, but many are partially natural. Plasticity is the general property of all materials that are able to irreversibly deform without breaking, but this occurs to such a degree with this class of moldable polymers that their name is an emphasis on this ability.

Childs.Title: BLACKBOARD
Childs.Definition: A blackboard (also known as a chalkboard) is a reusable writing surface on which text or drawings are made with sticks of calcium sulfate or calcium carbonate, known, when used for this purpose, as chalk. Blackboards were originally made of smooth, thin sheets of black or dark grey slate stone. Modern versions are often green because the colour is considered easier on the eyes.

Childs.Title: FRONT PROJECTION SCREEN
Childs.Definition: A front projection screen is an installation consisting of a surface and a support structure used for displaying a projected image from in front of the screen for the view of an audience. Projection screens may be permanently installed, as in a movie theater.

Childs.Title: PROJECTION SCREEN (FRONT AND REAR PROJECTION)

Projection screens may be permanently installed, as in a movie theater.

Childs.Title: Type of Material
Childs.Definition: Indicates, with reference to the product branding, labelling or packaging, the descriptive term that is used by the product manufacturer to identify the type of material from which the product is made.

Childs.Title: PLASTIC
Childs.Definition: Plastic is a material consisting of any of a wide range of synthetic or semi-synthetic organics that are malleable and can be molded into solid objects of diverse shapes. Plastics are typically organic polymers of high molecular mass, but they often contain other substances. They are usually synthetic, most commonly derived from petrochemicals, but many are partially natural. Plasticity is the general property of all materials that are able to irreversibly deform without breaking, but this occurs to such a degree with this class of moldable polymers that their name is an emphasis on this ability.

A tungsten carbide tipped circular saw blade cuts a crescent shaped hole (called the mouth) in the opposite edges of two pieces of wood and an oval-shaped, highly-dried and compressed wooden biscuit is covered with glue and placed in the slot. The two boards are then clamped together and bonded.
Childs.DefinitionExcludes: Excludes products such as jointers and planers.

Childs.Title: PLASTIC
Childs.Definition: Plastic is a material consisting of any of a wide range of synthetic or semi-synthetic organics that are malleable and can be molded into solid objects of diverse shapes. Plastics are typically organic polymers of high molecular mass, but they often contain other substances. They are usually synthetic, most commonly derived from petrochemicals, but many are partially natural. Plasticity is the general property of all materials that are able to irreversibly deform without breaking, but this occurs to such a degree with this class of moldable polymers that their name is an emphasis on this ability.
